title: PowerPoint Presentation Design
tagline: Plan, design and deliver talks people remember
summary: Learn the craft of presenting: plan the message, structure the slides, write words that work, use visuals honestly and deliver with confidence. Every module has a slide-studio lab that checks your deck.

modules.title: Plan before you open the software
modules.summary: Decide who the talk is for, what they should do afterwards, and the three points that get them there.
modules.outcome: You can write a one-sentence message, choose three supporting points and outline a talk on paper before opening any slide software.
modules.intro: Most bad presentations are not bad because of the slides. They are bad because the speaker never decided what the point was. Spend your first ten minutes with a pen and paper, and the slides will almost build themselves.

topics.title: Audience, purpose and the one-sentence message
topics.html:
Start with three questions. Who is listening, and what do they already know? Why are you speaking: to inform, persuade or teach? What should they think, feel or do when you finish?

Answer these before you start
QuestionExample
Who is the audience?Teachers and the principal, busy, not technical
What do they know?That students are often late, but not why
What do I want them to do?Approve a trial of a new gate timetable
How long do I have?Ten minutes plus questions
Definition

Core message. The one sentence you want the audience to remember. If they forgot everything else, this is what they should leave with.

Worked example

Write the core message

A student wants to ask for a bicycle shed.

  1. Weak: Bicycles at our school.
  2. Better: Our school needs a covered bicycle shed so more students can cycle safely.
  3. Test: could the audience repeat it? If not, make it shorter.

Answer. A good core message is a complete sentence that states what you want and why.

Tip

Write your message on a sticky note and keep it in view while you build the deck. Every slide should serve it.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a core message?
  • The longest slide
  • The title of the file
  • The one sentence you want remembered (correct)
  • The speaker's name

It is the single idea the audience should leave with.

2. Which is the best first step in preparing a talk?
  • Choose a theme
  • Pick fonts
  • Add animations
  • Decide the audience and purpose (correct)

Purpose comes before decoration.
keyPoints: Know your audience, purpose and the action you want.
A core message is one complete sentence.

topics.title: Structure: beginning, middle and end
topics.html:
Most talks work with three main points. People remember three things; they forget ten. Group your material under three headings and cut what does not fit.

A ten-minute talk
PartTimeSlides
Opening: hook and message1 minute1 to 2
Three main points7 minutes4 to 5
Close: summary and request2 minutes1 to 2
Watch out

A rough rule is one slide per minute or less. Fifteen slides in ten minutes means you are rushing.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with your name, your school and an apology.
  • Reading out a list of what you will cover for two minutes.
  • Ending with Thank you and nothing else.

Check what you just learned

1. How many main points does a short talk usually need?
  • Three (correct)
  • Ten
  • One slide only
  • As many as possible

Three is memorable.

2. Fifteen slides for ten minutes is:
  • Ideal
  • Probably too many (correct)
  • Required
  • Too few

More than about one slide a minute means rushing.
keyPoints: Hook, problem, idea, next step.
Three main points; about one slide per minute.

topics.title: Storyboarding on paper
topics.html:
A storyboard is a row of rough boxes, one per slide, where you write each slide's headline and sketch what it will show. It takes ten minutes and saves hours of rework.

How to storyboard

  1. Fold a sheet of paper into eight boxes.
  2. Write the headline of each slide at the top of its box.
  3. Sketch the picture, chart or diagram, or write the three key words.
  4. Read just the headlines in order: do they tell the whole story?
  5. Cut or merge any slide that does not help the message.
Worked example

Headlines that tell the story

A talk about plastic waste.

  1. 1. Our school throws away 40 kilograms a day
  2. 2. Most of it could be recycled
  3. 3. Students do not know which bin to use
  4. 4. Clear bins and a monitor can fix that
  5. 5. Please approve the trial

Answer. If the headlines read like a short argument, the talk will be easy to follow.

Try it yourself: Why should the headlines read like a story on their own?

Model answer. Because the audience mostly remembers the headlines, and a reader skimming the file should still get the argument.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a storyboard?
  • A finished deck
  • A theme
  • A rough plan of each slide's headline and picture (correct)
  • A script

It is a rough sketch plan.

Key terms: flip and sort

Audience
The people you are speaking to
Core message
The one sentence to remember
Hook
The opening that shows why it matters
Storyboard
A rough plan of each slide
Call to action
What you want people to do next
keyPoints: Storyboard on paper before using software.
The headlines alone should tell the story.

modules.title: Slide structure and layouts
modules.summary: Use layouts, themes and consistency to give every slide a clear job and a consistent look.
modules.outcome: You can choose the right layout for a slide, apply a theme and keep fonts, colours and positions consistent.
modules.intro: A deck should look like one object, not a collection of separate pages. Layouts and themes do most of that work for you, as long as you use them instead of working against them.

topics.title: The four layouts you need
topics.html:
Layouts and their jobs
LayoutJobExample
Title slideOpens or closes the talkCanteen orders: a plan from Class 9
Title and bulletsA point with a few supportsThree benefits of a reading hour
Two columnsA comparison or a pairBefore and after
Section headingDivides the talkPart two: the cost

Use title and bullets for most slides, and keep the others for moments where they add meaning. Do not change layouts only for variety: each change should signal that something is different.

Worked example

Choose the layouts for an eight-slide talk

A talk proposing a school garden has eight slides.

  1. Slide 1 uses the title layout for the talk's name.
  2. Slides 2 to 4 use title and bullets for the problem, the evidence and the idea.
  3. Slide 5 uses a section heading to mark the move from why to how.
  4. Slide 6 uses two columns to compare the costs and the benefits.
  5. Slides 7 and 8 use title and bullets for the plan and the request.

Answer. Mostly title and bullets, with the other layouts used only where they signal something: a start, a change of topic or a comparison.

Tip

If you find yourself fighting a layout, you probably chose the wrong one. Change it rather than moving boxes by hand.

Check what you just learned

1. Which layout suits a before-and-after comparison?
  • Title slide
  • Blank
  • Section heading
  • Two columns (correct)

Two columns put the two sides together.
keyPoints: Title, bullets, two columns and section cover most needs.
Choose a layout for its job, not for variety.

topics.title: Themes, fonts and colour
topics.html:
A theme sets the fonts, colours and background for the whole deck. Choose one at the start and keep it. Change a colour or font in the theme, not slide by slide, so every slide changes together.

Rules for a clean look

  1. One theme for the whole deck.
  2. Two fonts at most: one for titles, one for body text.
  3. A small palette: one main colour, one accent, plus black, white and grey.
  4. Strong contrast between text and background.
  5. Dark text on a light background for rooms with lights on; light on dark for dim rooms.
Watch out

Red text on a green background, or light grey on white, may be unreadable for people with colour vision differences or on a bright projector.

Check what you just learned

1. Where should you change fonts for the whole deck?
  • In the theme (correct)
  • On every slide
  • In the footer
  • In the file name

Theme settings apply across the deck.
keyPoints: One theme, two fonts, a small palette, strong contrast.
Change fonts and colours in the theme so every slide updates together.

topics.title: Consistency and alignment
topics.html:
The audience notices when a title jumps a few pixels between slides, even if they cannot say why. Keep titles in the same place, with the same size and colour, and keep margins consistent.

A consistency checklist
CheckWhy
Titles in the same positionThe eye does not need to search
Same bullet style everywhereLooks designed, not assembled
Same margin around contentA tidy frame
Same style for images and shapesFeels like one deck
Slide numbers (if used) in the same cornerHelps people refer to slides

Common mistakes

  • Moving a title by hand on one slide.
  • Mixing three kinds of bullet.
  • Pasting from another deck without matching its look.

Check what you just learned

1. Why keep titles in the same place?
  • It is a rule of the software
  • The audience does not have to search for them (correct)
  • It saves ink
  • It makes slides longer

A stable layout lets people focus on content.

Key terms: flip and sort

Layout
The arrangement of boxes on a slide
Theme
A set of fonts, colours and backgrounds
Contrast
Difference between text and background
Consistency
Using the same style everywhere
keyPoints: Keep titles, margins and styles identical across slides.
A tidy, consistent deck lets the audience focus on what you say.

modules.title: Words that work on a slide
modules.summary: Write headlines that make a point and keep text short enough to read in seconds.
modules.outcome: You can write headline sentences, trim bullets to key words and decide what goes on the slide and what you say aloud.
modules.intro: A slide is not a document. The audience will read it in about five seconds and then look back at you. This module is about saying less on the slide so that more of your message gets through.

topics.title: Headlines that make a point
topics.html:
A label tells the audience the topic: Sales. A headline tells them the point: Sales rose 20% after we changed the menu. Write your slide titles as short sentences that state the message of the slide.

Label versus headline
Label (weak)Headline (strong)
RecyclingMost of our school waste could be recycled
ResultsReading time doubled in one term
CostThe shed costs less than one new computer
PlanThree steps get bins in every class by May
Tip

Test a headline by covering the rest of the slide. If the title alone gives the point, it works.

Try it yourself: Rewrite the label Our survey as a headline for a survey where 6 in 10 students read nothing for fun.

Model answer. Six in ten students read nothing for fun.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a headline rather than a label?
  • Results
  • Next steps
  • Profit rose 12% this year (correct)
  • Introduction

It states the point.
keyPoints: A headline states the point; a label only names the topic.
Keep headlines to one short line.

topics.title: Less text, bigger text
topics.html:
Rules of readable text

  1. No more than four bullets per slide.
  2. No more than about six words per bullet.
  3. Body text at 24 points or larger so people at the back can read it.
  4. One idea per slide: if you need 'and', you probably need two slides.
  5. Full sentences go in your notes, not on the slide.
Worked example

Cut a bullet

Before: Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new objects.

  1. Find the key idea: waste becomes new things.
  2. Cut the filler words: the process of, converting.
  3. Result: Waste becomes new things.

Answer. Short bullets point to your idea; you say the rest aloud.

Watch out

If you could hand out the slide as a document and nobody would need you, it has too much text for a talk.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a sensible limit for bullets on a slide?
  • Twelve
  • None
  • Thirty
  • Four (correct)

Four is about the most people can scan at once.

2. Where do full sentences belong?
  • In your notes (correct)
  • On the slide
  • In the footer
  • In the theme

Speak them, or keep them in your notes.
keyPoints: Four bullets, six words each, body text 24 points or larger.
Put the detail in notes or a handout, not on the slide.

topics.title: Notes and handouts
topics.html:
Because slides are short, your detail needs a home. Put it in the speaker notes (for you) and in a handout (for the audience, given after the talk). Never hand it out before: people read ahead and stop listening.

What goes where
PlaceContents
The slideA headline, a picture, three to four key words
Speaker notesWhat you will say, numbers to remember, sources
HandoutFull data, references and contact details
Tip

Practise from your notes once, then try to speak from the slides alone. Notes are a safety net, not a script to read out.

Check what you just learned

1. When should a handout be given?
  • Before you start
  • After the talk (correct)
  • During every slide
  • Never

Give it afterwards so people listen first.

Key terms: flip and sort

Headline
A title that states the point
Label
A title that only names the topic
Speaker notes
Notes only the speaker sees
Handout
A document given to the audience after the talk
keyPoints: Notes are for you; handouts are for the audience, after the talk.
Keep the slide short and put the detail where it belongs.

modules.title: Visuals, shapes and data
modules.summary: Use pictures, diagrams and charts to show what words cannot, and keep them clean.
modules.outcome: You can choose a visual that suits the message, draw a simple process diagram with shapes and present numbers honestly.
modules.intro: People remember pictures better than words. But a picture must carry the message, not decorate it. This module is about choosing the visual that does the job, and drawing it simply.

topics.title: Choosing a visual
topics.html:
Match the visual to the message
MessageVisual
How a process worksA flow of boxes and arrows
How two things compareA bar chart or two columns
How something changes over timeA line chart
What something looks likeA photograph
How parts make up a wholeA pie chart with few parts
Watch out

Decoration is not visual. Clip art that only fills space distracts from your point; leave white space instead.

Worked example

Pick a visual

You want to show that a new bus route cut travel time from 50 minutes to 30.

  1. Message: the new route is faster.
  2. Comparison of two numbers, so use two bars or two columns.
  3. Label the bars with the minutes and start the axis at zero.
  4. Headline: The new route saves twenty minutes.

Answer. The right visual is the simplest one that shows the comparison without extra decoration.

Tip

Ask of every picture: what does it show that my words do not? If the answer is nothing, delete it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which visual shows how a process works?
  • A pie chart
  • A photo of a face
  • Boxes joined by arrows (correct)
  • A table of names

A flow diagram follows the steps.
keyPoints: Choose the visual for the message.
Delete decoration.

topics.title: Drawing a simple diagram
topics.html:
How to draw a clean diagram

  1. Use one shape for one idea: a box for a step, an arrow for the flow.
  2. Keep the same size and spacing between boxes.
  3. Put short words inside the shapes, not sentences.
  4. Use one accent colour to highlight the most important step.
  5. Align shapes in a row or a column, never at random angles.

Common mistakes

  • Shapes of many colours with no meaning.
  • Long text inside a box that does not fit.
  • Arrows that cross each other.

Check what you just learned

1. What should text inside a diagram box be?
  • A paragraph
  • A URL
  • Empty
  • A few words (correct)

Keep text inside shapes short.
keyPoints: One shape, one idea; align and space evenly.
Keep words inside shapes to one or two, and highlight only the key step.

topics.title: Showing numbers honestly
topics.html:
A chart is persuasive, so it carries a duty to be fair. Start bars at zero, label what is measured and give the source.

Honest charts

  • Bars start at zero, or the difference is exaggerated.
  • Label the axis or the bars with the unit.
  • One message per chart; state it in the headline.
  • Avoid 3D effects; they distort sizes.
  • Cite the source of the data.
Worked example

A headline for a chart

A bar chart shows 8 cyclists this year and 6 last year.

  1. Do not write Cycling numbers.
  2. Write: Cycling rose from 6 to 8 students out of 100.
  3. Say aloud that it is a small change but a start.

Answer. A chart headline states the finding and the scale, so the audience is not misled.

Check what you just learned

1. Why start a bar chart at zero?
  • A cut-off axis exaggerates differences (correct)
  • It looks tidier
  • It is faster
  • It adds colour

Truncated bars mislead.

Key terms: flip and sort

Diagram
A picture of how something works
Alignment
Lining up shapes along a line
Chart
A picture of numbers
Source
Where the data came from
keyPoints: Start bars at zero, label units, one message per chart.
Write the chart headline as the finding, and cite the source.

modules.title: Story and delivery
modules.summary: Open with a hook, move through your points with clear transitions, and speak with confidence.
modules.outcome: You can open a talk strongly, link ideas smoothly, rehearse effectively and handle questions.
modules.intro: The best deck cannot rescue a poor delivery, and a confident speaker can survive an ordinary deck. This module covers what you say and how you say it.

topics.title: Openings and closings
topics.html:
Ways to open
OpeningExample
A surprising numberForty kilograms of waste leave our school every day.
A short storyLast Monday I watched a student carry a full lunch to the bin.
A questionHow many of you have ever been unsure which bin to use?
A bold promiseIn ten minutes I will show you how to halve our waste.

Your close matters as much as your opening. End with a summary of your three points and a specific request. Do not trail off with 'that is all'; finish on your ask, then say thank you.

Tip

Memorise your first and last sentences. Starting and finishing strongly makes the middle easier.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a strong opening?
  • Sorry, I am nervous
  • Forty kilograms of waste leave our school every day (correct)
  • Today I will talk about waste
  • Um, hello

A striking fact grabs attention.
keyPoints: Open with a number, story, question or promise.
Close with a summary and a request.

topics.title: Transitions and signposting
topics.html:
Signposts tell the audience where they are in the talk: 'First, the problem. Second, our plan. Third, the cost.' Transitions link one slide to the next: 'That is the problem. So what can we do?'

Useful signposts

  • First, second and finally.
  • That is the problem. Now the solution.
  • So what does this mean for us?
  • Let me summarise the three points.
Worked example

Link two slides

Slide 3 ends the problem; slide 4 starts the plan.

  1. Say: So that is what is wrong. Here is what we can do about it.
  2. Click to the next slide only after saying it.
  3. The audience hears the link before the new slide appears.

Answer. A one-sentence bridge keeps the talk flowing.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a signpost?
  • A slide number
  • A theme
  • A phrase that tells people where you are in the talk (correct)
  • An animation

It orients the audience.
keyPoints: Signposts tell people where they are; transitions link the slides.
Say the bridge sentence before you click to the next slide.

topics.title: Voice, rehearsal and questions
topics.html:
Delivery habits

  1. Speak a little slower than feels natural.
  2. Pause after each key point.
  3. Look at people, not at the screen.
  4. Stand to one side so nobody's view is blocked.
  5. Use your hands naturally; do not hide them.
Handling questions
SituationWhat to do
You know the answerAnswer briefly, then check you answered it
You do not knowSay so, and promise to find out
A long or off-topic questionOffer to talk afterwards
A hostile questionStay calm; thank them; answer the fair part

Nerves are normal and mostly invisible to the audience. Slow your breathing before you start, plant your feet, and focus on helping the audience rather than on being judged. A speaker who is slightly nervous but well prepared always beats one who is fluent but has nothing to say.

Watch out

Never apologise for your slides. If something goes wrong, carry on calmly: the audience will follow your lead.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the best response to a question you cannot answer?
  • Make something up
  • Change the subject
  • Ignore it
  • Say you do not know and promise to find out (correct)

Honesty builds trust.

2. How can rehearsal help?
  • It shows timing and awkward phrases (correct)
  • It changes the theme
  • It deletes slides
  • It is optional

Spoken rehearsal reveals problems.

Key terms: flip and sort

Hook
A strong opening
Signpost
A phrase that tells people where they are
Transition
A link between two ideas
Rehearsal
Practising out loud
keyPoints: Speak slowly, pause, look up, rehearse aloud.
It is fine to say you do not know.

modules.title: Review and present
modules.summary: Check a deck against a simple list, make it accessible, and present it well in person or online.
modules.outcome: You can review a deck against a checklist, export it for sharing and present confidently face to face or remotely.
modules.intro: The last ten percent of the work decides how professional a talk looks. This module gives you a checklist and some habits for the day itself.

topics.title: A review checklist
topics.html:
Review checklist

  1. Does the deck serve one core message?
  2. Do the headlines alone tell the story?
  3. Is any slide overloaded? Cut it.
  4. Are fonts and colours consistent, and is the contrast strong?
  5. Is every chart honest and labelled?
  6. Are spelling, names and numbers correct?
  7. Does the first slide say what the talk is, and the last say what to do?
Typical problems and fixes
ProblemFix
Too many slidesMerge or delete the weakest
Dense textCut to key words; move detail to notes
Inconsistent lookApply the theme; fix positions
TyposRead aloud; ask a friend
Worked example

Review one slide

A slide titled Recycling has nine bullets in small text and a clip-art bin.

  1. Message check: what is the point? The title does not say.
  2. Density check: nine bullets is too many; keep the strongest three.
  3. Visual check: the clip art decorates only; replace it with a number such as 40 kg a day.
  4. New headline: Our school throws away 40 kilograms a day.

Answer. A good review leaves a slide with one point, a few words and one purposeful visual.

Tip

Review with a friend who has not seen it. If they cannot tell you the message after one pass, the deck needs work.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a quick test of a deck's clarity?
  • Count the colours
  • Ask someone new to state the message (correct)
  • Check file size
  • Time the animations

A fresh viewer reveals unclear points.
keyPoints: Check message, headlines, density, consistency, honesty and typos.
Ask someone new to the deck to state the message after one pass.

topics.title: Accessible and shareable decks
topics.html:
Make a deck accessible

  1. Use real layouts so titles are readable by screen readers.
  2. Add a short description to every picture.
  3. Use large text and strong contrast.
  4. Do not put key information in colour alone.
  5. Provide the handout or notes for people who need more time.
Sharing choices
GoalChoose
People will present itShare the editable deck
People will read itExport a PDF handout
Large audienceShare a link with view-only access
Watch out

Remove speaker notes with private comments before you share the file.

Check what you just learned

1. What should every picture have for accessibility?
  • A frame
  • A border
  • A short description (correct)
  • A shadow

It lets screen readers describe it.
keyPoints: Accessible decks use real layouts, picture descriptions and strong contrast.
Share a PDF to read, an editable file to present, a view-only link for large groups.

topics.title: Presenting in a room and online
topics.html:
In person and online
SituationTips
In a roomArrive early, test the projector and a spare cable; stand beside the screen; keep eye contact
OnlineTest sound and camera; close other tabs; look at the camera; keep slides even simpler; invite questions in chat

Common mistakes

  • Not checking the equipment before the audience arrives.
  • Talking to the screen.
  • Running over time.

Check what you just learned

1. When presenting online you should look at:
  • Your own face
  • The ceiling
  • The keyboard
  • The camera (correct)

The camera feels like eye contact.

Key terms: flip and sort

Checklist
A list of things to verify
Alt text
A description of an image
Handout
A document for the audience
View-only link
A link that does not allow edits
keyPoints: Test equipment early; online, look at the camera and simplify.
Never apologise for your slides; carry on calmly if something fails.

steps: Work through the Final project: a ten-minute talk lab with a clear problem, a plan, a diagram and a next-steps slide.
Practise it aloud twice and time it.
Take the final assessment below.
